claim: The endoderm has been proposed to be the most ancient of the three embryonic germ layers in metazoans.
source: The endoderm has been proposed to be the most ancient of the three embryonic germ layers in metazoans (Hashimshony et al., 2015; Rodaway and Patient, 2001), having appeared prior to the advent of the Bilateria about 600 Mya (Peterson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hashimshony et al., 2015; Rodaway and Patient, 2001; Peterson et al., 2004).

claim: The endoderm appeared prior to the advent of the Bilateria about 600 Mya.
source: The endoderm has been proposed to be the most ancient of the three embryonic germ layers in metazoans (Hashimshony et al., 2015; Rodaway and Patient, 2001), having appeared prior to the advent of the Bilateria about 600 Mya (Peterson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Peterson et al., 2004).

claim: The core transcriptional machinery for endoderm specification and differentiation appears to share common mechanisms across metazoan phylogeny.
source: However, the core transcriptional machinery for endoderm specification and differentiation appears to share common mechanisms across metazoan phylogeny.
evidence: Supported by subsequent examples and citations in the text describing GATA factors across species.

claim: Cascades of GATA-type transcription factors function to promote endoderm development in triploblastic animals and the most basal metazoans that contain a digestive tract.
source: For example, cascades of GATA-type transcription factors function to promote endoderm development not only in triploblastic animals but also in the most basal metazoans that contain a digestive tract (Martindale et al., 2004; Boyle and Seaver, 2008; Boyle and Seaver, 2010; Gillis et al., 2007; Davidson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature (Martindale et al., 2004; Boyle and Seaver, 2008; Boyle and Seaver, 2010; Gillis et al., 2007; Davidson et al., 2002).

claim: The endoderm-determining GATA factor END-1 in C. elegans is sufficient to activate endoderm development in cells that would otherwise become ectoderm in Xenopus.
source: Among the many observations supporting a common regulatory mechanism for establishing the endoderm, it has been found that the endoderm-determining GATA factor, END-1, in the nematode C. elegans, is sufficient to activate endoderm development in cells that would otherwise become ectoderm in Xenopus (Shoichet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Shoichet et al., 2000).

claim: The role of GATA factors in endoderm development has been preserved since nematodes and vertebrates diverged from a common ancestor that lived perhaps 600 Mya.
source: This indicates that the role of GATA factors in endoderm development has been preserved since the nematodes and vertebrates diverged from a common ancestor that lived perhaps 600 Mya.
evidence: Based on inference from the cross-species functional conservation of GATA factors and estimated divergence time.

claim: The E cell in C. elegans is the progenitor of the entire endoderm, which subsequently gives rise exclusively to the intestine.
source: The E cell, which is produced in the very early C. elegans embryo, is the progenitor of the entire endoderm, which subsequently gives rise exclusively to the intestine.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The EMS blastomere at the four-cell stage divides to produce the E founder cell and its anterior sister, the MS founder cell.
source: The EMS blastomere at the four-cell stage divides to produce the E founder cell and its anterior sister, the MS founder cell, which is the progenitor for much of the mesoderm (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Sulston et al., 1983).

claim: Both E and MS fates are determined by maternally provided SKN-1, an orthologue of the vertebrate Nrf2 bZIP transcription factor.
source: Both E and MS fates are determined by maternally provided SKN-1, an orthologue of the vertebrate Nrf2 bZIP transcription factor (Bowerman et al., 1992; Bowerman et al., 1993; Maduro and Rothman, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bowerman et al., 1992; Bowerman et al., 1993; Maduro and Rothman, 2002).

claim: Elimination of maternal SKN-1 function in the laboratory N2 strain results in fully penetrant embryonic lethality as a result of misspecification of EMS cell descendants.
source: In the laboratory N2 strain, elimination of maternal SKN-1 function (through either knockdown or knockout) results in fully penetrant embryonic lethality as a result of misspecification of EMS cell descendants.
evidence: Established knowledge about SKN-1 function in C. elegans N2 strain.

claim: In skn-1(-) embryos, the fate of MS is transformed to that of its cousin, the mesectodermal progenitor C cell.
source: In these embryos, the fate of MS is transformed to that of its cousin, the mesectodermal progenitor C cell.
evidence: Established knowledge about SKN-1 function in C. elegans.

claim: E cells adopt a C cell-like fate in a majority, but not all, of skn-1(-) embryos.
source: E cells similarly adopt a C cell-like fate in a majority, but not all, of these embryos (Bowerman et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bowerman et al., 1992).

claim: SKN-1 initiates mesendoderm development via the GRN in E and MS cells in part by activating zygotic expression of the MED-1/2 divergent GATA transcription factors.
source: SKN-1 initiates mesendoderm development via the GRN in E and MS cells in part by activating zygotic expression of the MED-1/2 divergent GATA transcription factors (Maduro et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Maduro et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2001).

claim: MED-1/2 mobilizes a cascade of GATA factors in the E cell lineage that ultimately direct intestinal differentiation.
source: This event mobilizes a cascade of GATA factors in the E cell lineage that ultimately direct intestinal differentiation (Maduro and Rothman, 2002; Maduro, 2017; Wiesenfahrt et al., 2016; McGhee, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Maduro and Rothman, 2002; Maduro, 2017; Wiesenfahrt et al., 2016; McGhee, 2007).

claim: The differential requirement for SKN-1 in endoderm (E) and mesoderm (MS) development is determined by its combinatorial action with triply redundant Wnt, MAPK, and Src signaling systems.
source: This differential requirement for SKN-1 in endoderm (E) and mesoderm (MS) development is determined by its combinatorial action with triply redundant Wnt, MAPK, and Src signaling systems, which act together to polarize EMS (Meneghini et al., 1999; Shin et al., 1999; Bei et al., 2002; Thorpe et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Meneghini et al., 1999; Shin et al., 1999; Bei et al., 2002; Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: MOM-2/Wnt acts through the MOM-5/Frizzled receptor, mobilizing WRM-1/β-catenin, resulting in its cytoplasmic accumulation in the posterior side of EMS.
source: MOM-2/Wnt acts through the MOM-5/Frizzled receptor, mobilizing WRM-1/β-catenin, resulting in its cytoplasmic accumulation in the posterior side of EMS.
evidence: Established knowledge about Wnt signaling in C. elegans.

claim: WRM-1, together with LIT-1/NLK kinase, alters both the nucleocytoplasmic distribution and activity of the Wnt effector POP-1/Tcf.
source: WRM-1, together with LIT-1/NLK kinase, alters both the nucleocytoplasmic distribution and activity of the Wnt effector POP-1/Tcf (Thorpe et al., 1997; Nakamura et al., 2005; Rocheleau et al., 1999), converting it from a repressor of endoderm in the MS cell lineage to an activator in the E cell lineage (Owraghi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2002; Phillips et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2005a; Shetty et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Thorpe et al., 1997; Nakamura et al., 2005; Rocheleau et al., 1999; Owraghi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2002; Phillips et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2005a; Shetty et al., 2005).

claim: POP-1 is converted from a repressor of endoderm in the MS cell lineage to an activator in the E cell lineage.
source: WRM-1, together with LIT-1/NLK kinase, alters both the nucleocytoplasmic distribution and activity of the Wnt effector POP-1/Tcf (Thorpe et al., 1997; Nakamura et al., 2005; Rocheleau et al., 1999), converting it from a repressor of endoderm in the MS cell lineage to an activator in the E cell lineage (Owraghi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2002; Phillips et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2005a; Shetty et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Owraghi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2002; Phillips et al., 2007; Maduro et al., 2005a; Shetty et al., 2005).

claim: Loss of MOM-2 expression in the laboratory N2 strain results in a partial gutless phenotype.
source: Loss of MOM-2 expression in the laboratory N2 strain results in a partial gutless phenotype, while removal of both MOM-2 and SKN-1, through either knockdown or knockout, leads to a completely penetrant loss of gut (Thorpe et al., 1997), revealing their genetically redundant roles.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: Removal of both MOM-2 and SKN-1 leads to a completely penetrant loss of gut.
source: Loss of MOM-2 expression in the laboratory N2 strain results in a partial gutless phenotype, while removal of both MOM-2 and SKN-1, through either knockdown or knockout, leads to a completely penetrant loss of gut (Thorpe et al., 1997), revealing their genetically redundant roles.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: MOM-2 and SKN-1 have genetically redundant roles in endoderm specification.
source: Loss of MOM-2 expression in the laboratory N2 strain results in a partial gutless phenotype, while removal of both MOM-2 and SKN-1, through either knockdown or knockout, leads to a completely penetrant loss of gut (Thorpe et al., 1997), revealing their genetically redundant roles.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of both factors is required for complete penetrance, supported by citation (Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: The regulatory relationship between SKN-1 and POP-1 shows substantial variation even in species that diverged 20–40 million years ago.
source: The regulatory relationship between SKN-1 and POP-1, the effector of Wnt signaling, shows substantial variation even in species that diverged 20–40 million years ago, suggesting significant evolutionary plasticity in this key node in the endoderm GRN.
evidence: Supported by subsequent description of differences between C. elegans and C. briggsae.

claim: C. elegans embryos lacking maternal POP-1 always make gut, both in the normal E cell lineage and in the MS cell lineage.
source: C. elegans embryos lacking maternal POP-1 always make gut, both in the normal E cell lineage and in the MS cell lineage.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: In C. elegans embryos lacking both SKN-1 and POP-1, endoderm is virtually never made.
source: However, in embryos lacking both SKN-1 and POP-1, endoderm is virtually never made, implying that these two factors constitute a Boolean 'OR' logic gate.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: SKN-1 and POP-1 constitute a Boolean 'OR' logic gate in C. elegans.
source: However, in embryos lacking both SKN-1 and POP-1, endoderm is virtually never made, implying that these two factors constitute a Boolean 'OR' logic gate.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of either factor alone allows gut formation, but loss of both prevents it.

claim: Removal of either SKN-1 or POP-1 alone in C. briggsae causes >90% of embryos to lack gut.
source: In contrast, removal of either SKN-1 or POP-1 alone in C. briggsae causes >90% of embryos to lack gut, indicative of an 'AND' logic gate (Figure 1A,B) (Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Lin et al., 2009) and reference to Figure 1A,B.

claim: SKN-1 and POP-1 constitute an 'AND' logic gate in C. briggsae.
source: In contrast, removal of either SKN-1 or POP-1 alone in C. briggsae causes >90% of embryos to lack gut, indicative of an 'AND' logic gate (Figure 1A,B) (Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of either factor alone prevents gut formation in C. briggsae, supported by citation (Lin et al., 2009) and Figure 1A,B.

claim: RNAi of skn-1 in different N2-derived mutant strains gave highly reproducible results with 100% of the embryos arresting.
source: In our experimental conditions, we found that RNAi of skn-1 in different N2-derived mutant strains gave highly reproducible results: 100% of the embryos derived from skn-1(RNAi)-treated mothers arrest (n > 100,000) and 32.0 ± 1.9% of the arrested embryos exhibited birefringent gut granules (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1) over many trials by separate investigators.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (n > 100,000) and Figure 2A.

claim: 32.0 ± 1.9% of arrested skn-1(RNAi) embryos in N2 exhibited birefringent gut granules.
source: In our experimental conditions, we found that RNAi of skn-1 in different N2-derived mutant strains gave highly reproducible results: 100% of the embryos derived from skn-1(RNAi)-treated mothers arrest (n > 100,000) and 32.0 ± 1.9% of the arrested embryos exhibited birefringent gut granules (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1) over many trials by separate investigators.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and Figure 2A.

claim: The LSJ1 laboratory strain gave virtually identical results to N2 for skn-1(RNAi) (31.0% ± s.d 1.2%).
source: We found that the LSJ1 laboratory strain, which is derived from the same original source as N2, but experienced very different selective pressures in the laboratory owing to its constant propagation in liquid culture over 40 years (Sterken et al., 2015), gave virtually identical results to that of N2 (31.0% ± s.d 1.2%), implying that SKN-1-independent endoderm formation is a quantitatively stable trait.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SKN-1-independent endoderm formation is a quantitatively stable trait.
source: We found that the LSJ1 laboratory strain, which is derived from the same original source as N2, but experienced very different selective pressures in the laboratory owing to its constant propagation in liquid culture over 40 years (Sterken et al., 2015), gave virtually identical results to that of N2 (31.0% ± s.d 1.2%), implying that SKN-1-independent endoderm formation is a quantitatively stable trait.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that N2 and LSJ1 show similar phenotypes despite different selective pressures.

claim: The effects of skn-1(RNAi) varied dramatically across C. elegans wild isolates, ranging from 0.9% to 60% of embryos with differentiated gut.
source: However, we observed dramatic variation in the fraction of embryos with differentiated gut across the complete set of strains, ranging from 0.9% to 60% (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: All wild isolates, with the exception of the RNAi-resistant Hawaiian CB4856 strain, invariably gave 100% embryonic lethality with skn-1(RNAi).
source: We found that all strains, with the exception of the RNAi-resistant Hawaiian CB4856 strain, invariably gave 100% embryonic lethality with skn-1(RNAi).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some wild isolates that were subsequently found to have identical genome sequences also gave identical skn-1(RNAi) results.
source: Further, we found that some wild isolates that were subsequently found to have identical genome sequences also gave identical results.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Embryos from all strains showed a decisive 'all-or-none' phenotype for gut differentiation.
source: We note that embryos from all strains showed a decisive 'all-or-none' phenotype: that is, they were either strongly positive for gut differentiation or completely lacked gut granules, with virtually no intermediate or ambiguous phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: A threshold of gene activity in the GRN accounts for the all-or-none switch in gut specification.
source: A threshold of gene activity in the GRN has been shown to account for such an all-or-none switch in gut specification (Maduro et al., 2007; Raj et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Maduro et al., 2007; Raj et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 1997).

claim: The fraction of embryos containing immunoreactive IFB-2 was not significantly different from the fraction containing gut granules in selected strains.
source: In all cases, we found that the fraction of embryos containing immunoreactive IFB-2 was not significantly different (Fisher's exact test, p-values>0.05) from the fraction containing gut granules, strongly suggesting that the strains vary in endoderm specification per se and consistent with earlier studies of SKN-1 function (Bowerman et al., 1992; Maduro et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Fisher's exact test, p-values>0.05) and citations (Bowerman et al., 1992; Maduro et al., 2007).

claim: The strains vary in endoderm specification per se.
source: In all cases, we found that the fraction of embryos containing immunoreactive IFB-2 was not significantly different (Fisher's exact test, p-values>0.05) from the fraction containing gut granules, strongly suggesting that the strains vary in endoderm specification per se and consistent with earlier studies of SKN-1 function (Bowerman et al., 1992; Maduro et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IFB-2 and gut granules show consistent results, supported by data and citations.

claim: Introgression of the skn-1(zu67) allele through five rounds of backcrosses resulted in a quantitative phenotype that was similar or indistinguishable from that observed with skn-1(RNAi) in most strains.
source: In all cases, we found that introgression of the allele through five rounds of backcrosses resulted in a quantitative phenotype that was similar or indistinguishable from that observed with skn-1(RNAi).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The phenotypes of the introgressed skn-1(zu67) allele were significantly different from that of the parental N2 skn-1(zu67) strain, except for DL238.
source: The phenotypes of the introgressed allele were significantly different (p-values<0.01) from that of the parental N2 skn-1(zu67) strain, except for DL238, whose skn-1(RNAi) phenotype was indistinguishable from that of N2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (p-values<0.01).

claim: The extreme variation in skn-1(RNAi) phenotype between the wild isolates tested results from bona fide cryptic variation in the endoderm GRN, rather than differences in RNAi efficacy.
source: We conclude that the extreme variation in skn-1(RNAi) phenotype between the wild isolates tested results from bona fide cryptic variation in the endoderm GRN, rather than differences in RNAi efficacy.
evidence: Inferred from the introgression experiments showing similar phenotypes with chromosomal mutations.

claim: The strength of skn-1(RNAi) phenotype does not correlate with phylogenetic relatedness between the strains (Pagel's λ = 0.42, p-value=0.14).
source: We note that the strength of skn-1(RNAi) phenotype does not correlate with phylogenetic relatedness between the strains (Pagel's λ = 0.42, p-value=0.14).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Pagel's λ = 0.42, p-value=0.14).

claim: Some closely related strains showed a similar skn-1(RNAi) phenotype, while other very closely related strains showed phenotypes on the opposite ends of the phenotypic spectrum.
source: For example, while some closely related strains (e.g., MY16 and MY23) showed a similar phenotype, other very closely related strains (e.g., JU1491 and JU778) showed phenotypes on the opposite ends of the phenotypic spectrum (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: There is no clear association between geographical distribution and skn-1(RNAi) phenotype.
source: We also did not observe any clear association between geographical distribution and skn-1 (RNAi) phenotype (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The initiating inputs into the endoderm GRN are subject to rapid intraspecies evolutionary divergence.
source: These findings suggest that the initiating inputs into the endoderm GRN is subject to rapid intraspecies evolutionary divergence.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between phylogenetic relatedness and phenotype.

claim: Broad variation in the requirement for MOM-2/Wnt in activation of the endoderm GRN was observed between isotypes.
source: Indeed, we observed broad variation in the requirement for MOM-2/Wnt in activation of the endoderm GRN between isotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mom-2(RNAi) of 94 isotypes resulted in embryonic arrest.
source: mom-2(RNAi) of 94 isotypes resulted in embryonic arrest, indicating that, as with skn-1(RNAi), mom-2(RNAi) was effective at least by the criterion of lethality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of mom-2(RNAi) embryos with differentiated gut varied from ~40% to ~99% in affected strains.
source: In the affected strains, the fraction of mom-2(RNAi) embryos with differentiated gut varied from ~40% to~99% (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Birefringence of gut granules is a reliable proxy for endoderm formation.
source: As with skn-1(RNAi), the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype of isotypes N2, JU440, and JU1213 was further confirmed by immunostaining with IFB-2 (Figure 4B), again demonstrating that birefringence of gut granules is a reliable proxy for endoderm formation for this analysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The introgression of mom-2(or42) into the N2 strain results in only ~28% of embryos showing endoderm differentiation.
source: In contrast, the introgression of an apparent loss-of-function allele, mom-2(or42), into the N2 strain results in a more extreme phenotype: only ~28% of embryos show endoderm differentiation (Figure 4C) (Thorpe et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and citation (Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: The mom-2(or42) allele introgressed into the isotype JU1213 background resulted in a low fraction of arrested embryos with gut (5.7% ± s.d 2.4%; n = 2292).
source: For example, the mom-2(or42) allele introgressed into the isotype JU1213 background resulted in a low fraction of arrested embryos with gut (5.7% ± s.d 2.4%; n = 2292), a more extreme effect than was seen with RNAi (34.0% ± s.d 1.5%; n = 1876).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mom-2(or42) phenotype in JU1213 is the strongest phenotype that has been reported for any known mom-2 allele.
source: This is the strongest phenotype that has been reported for any known mom-2 allele.
evidence: Based on comparison with published literature and experimental data.

claim: Introgression of the mom-2 mutation gave rise to a significantly higher fraction of embryos with endoderm in isotypes DL226 and PB303, relative to the laboratory strain N2.
source: On the other hand, introgression of the mom-2 mutation gave rise to a significantly higher fraction of embryos with endoderm in isotypes DL226 (55.2% ± s.d 1.2%, n = 1377) and PB303 (65.5% ± s.d 4.9%, n = 2726), relative to the laboratory strain N2 (29.1% ± s.d 3.1%; n = 1693), consistent with the RNAi phenotypes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The differential requirement for MOM-2 is, at least in part, attributable to genetic modifiers in these strains.
source: These findings indicate that the differential requirement for MOM-2 is, at least in part, attributable to genetic modifiers in these strains.
evidence: Inferred from the introgression experiments showing strain-specific differences.

claim: There is no correlation between the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype and phylogenetic relatedness or geographical distribution.
source: As with skn-1(RNAi), we found no correlation between the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype and phylogenetic relatedness or geographical distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting rapid intraspecies developmental system drift.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: pop-1(RNAi) resulted in 100% embryonic lethality across all 96 RNAi-sensitive isolates.
source: We found that, while pop-1(RNAi) resulted in 100% embryonic lethality across all 96 RNAi-sensitive isolates, 100% of the arrested embryos contained a differentiated gut (n > 500 for each isolate scored) (results not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 100% of arrested pop-1(RNAi) embryos contained a differentiated gut across all 96 RNAi-sensitive isolates.
source: We found that, while pop-1(RNAi) resulted in 100% embryonic lethality across all 96 RNAi-sensitive isolates, 100% of the arrested embryos contained a differentiated gut (n > 500 for each isolate scored) (results not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All isolates behave similarly to the N2 strain with respect to the requirement for POP-1.
source: Thus, all isolates behave similarly to the N2 strain with respect to the requirement for POP-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all isolates show 100% gut formation in pop-1(RNAi) embryos.

claim: The lack of variation in endoderm specification after loss of POP-1 is not entirely unexpected.
source: The lack of variation in endoderm specification after loss of POP-1 is not entirely unexpected.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about POP-1 function.

claim: Elimination of the endoderm-repressive role of POP-1 in the MS lineage supersedes its endoderm activating role in the presence of SKN-1.
source: As has been observed in a pop-1(-) mutant strain, elimination of the endoderm-repressive role of POP-1 in the MS lineage (which is not influenced by the P2 signal) supersedes its endoderm activating role in the presence of SKN-1.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about POP-1 function.

claim: The activating function for POP-1 is apparent only in the absence of SKN-1.
source: Indeed, the original observation that all pop-1(-) embryos in an N2 background contain gut masked the activating function for POP-1, which is apparent only in the absence of SKN-1 (Owraghi et al., 2010; Maduro et al., 2002; Maduro et al., 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Owraghi et al., 2010; Maduro et al., 2002; Maduro et al., 2005a).

claim: GWAS identified two significant closely-located positions on chromosome IV that underlie the variation in SKN-1 requirement.
source: This approach identified two significant closely-located positions on chromosome IV that underlie the variation in SKN-1 requirement (Figure 5A, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis presented in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: GWAS of the mom-2(RNAi) variation did not reveal any genomic regions that exceeded an FDR of 5%.
source: GWAS of the mom-2(RNAi) variation proved more challenging because this phenotype showed a highly skewed distribution (Shapiro-Wilk' test W = 0.8682, p-value=1.207×10−7) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). While GWAS did not reveal any genomic regions for the mom-2(RNAi) variation that exceeded an FDR of 5%, we found that the most strongly associated loci for the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype also showed large effects for skn-1(RNAi) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis and statistical test (Shapiro-Wilk' test W = 0.8682, p-value=1.207×10−7) presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most strongly associated loci for the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype also showed large effects for skn-1(RNAi).
source: While GWAS did not reveal any genomic regions for the mom-2(RNAi) variation that exceeded an FDR of 5%, we found that the most strongly associated loci for the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype also showed large effects for skn-1(RNAi) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Substantial overlap in the p-values for individual SNPs from skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) was observed in the central region of chromosome IV.
source: In particular, we observed substantial overlap in the p-values for individual SNPs from skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) in the central region of chromosome IV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), raising the possibility that common genetic factors might underlie these phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Common genetic factors might underlie the skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes.
source: In particular, we observed substantial overlap in the p-values for individual SNPs from skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) in the central region of chromosome IV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), raising the possibility that common genetic factors might underlie these phenotypes.
evidence: Speculative inference based on GWAS analysis.

claim: The skn-1(RNAi) phenotype varied widely across the RILs, with 1% to 47% of embryos containing gut.
source: For skn-1(RNAi), the phenotype varied widely across the RILs, with 1% to 47% of embryos containing gut (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes ranged from RILs showing 3% of embryos with gut to those showing 92%.
source: The mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes ranged from RILs showing 3% of embryos with gut to those showing 92% (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: In all RILs, skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) resulted in 100% lethality.
source: In all RILs, skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) resulted in 100% lethality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One RIL (JR3572) showed a nearly completely penetrant gutless phenotype with mom-2(RNAi), an effect that is much stronger than has been previously observed for mom-2(-).
source: It is noteworthy that one RIL (JR3572, Supplementary file 2) showed a nearly completely penetrant gutless phenotype, an effect that is much stronger than has been previously observed for mom-2(-) (Thorpe et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison with published literature (Thorpe et al., 1997).

claim: A combination of natural variants can nearly eliminate a requirement for MOM-2 altogether.
source: These results indicate that a combination of natural variants can nearly eliminate a requirement for MOM-2 altogether, while others make it virtually essential for endoderm development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of extreme phenotypes in RILs.

claim: Multiple quantitative trait loci (QTL) underlie SKN-1- and MOM-2-dependent endoderm specification.
source: Collectively, these analyses reveal that multiple quantitative trait loci (QTL) underlie SKN-1- and MOM-2-dependent endoderm specification.
evidence: Inferred from the QTL mapping results.

claim: For skn-1(RNAi), two major peaks were revealed on chromosomes II and IV (above 1% FDR).
source: For skn-1(RNAi), two major peaks were revealed on chromosomes II and IV (above 1% FDR estimated from 1000 permutations).
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Two minor loci for skn-1(RNAi) were found on chromosomes I and X (suggestive linkage, above 20% FDR).
source: Two minor loci were found on chromosomes I and X (suggestive linkage, above 20% FDR) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: For mom-2(RNAi), two major independent QTL peaks were found on chromosomes I and II (above the 5% FDR).
source: For mom-2(RNAi), two major independent QTL peaks were found on chromosomes I and II (above the 5% FDR estimated from 1000 permutations).
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Overlap was observed between the chromosomes I and II candidate regions for skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes.
source: Although the candidate peaks observed on chromosome IV for skn-1(RNAi) did not appear to overlap with those for mom-2(RNAi), overlap was observed between the chromosomes I and II candidate regions for these two phenotypes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: No strong relationship was found between the cryptic variation in the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 across all the strains (Spearman correlation R = 0.18, p-value=0.07).
source: This analysis revealed no strong relationship between the cryptic variation in the requirement for these inputs seen across all the strains (Spearman correlation R = 0.18, p-value=0.07) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Spearman correlation R = 0.18, p-value=0.07) presented in Figure 7A.

claim: A weak positive correlation (Pearson's R = 0.21, p=p value<2.2e-16) was found between the allelic effects of skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) across the genome.
source: We found a weak positive correlation (Pearson's R = 0.21, p=p value<2.2e-16, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) between the allelic effects.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Pearson's R = 0.21, p=p value<2.2e-16) presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between the skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes across the N2/MY16 RILs genome (genome-wide Pearson's R = −0.35, p=0.001).
source: In contrast, analysis of the N2/MY16 RILs uncovered a potential reciprocal relationship between the requirements for SKN-1 and MOM-2: we observed a negative correlation between the skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi) phenotypes across the genome (Figure 7B, genome-wide Pearson's R = −0.35, p=0.001, correcting for LD and outliers as above; correlation without chromosome IV R = −0.59, p<0.001) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Pearson's R = −0.35, p=0.001) presented in Figure 7B.

claim: At least some quantitative variants result in opposing effects on the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2.
source: This finding suggested that at least some quantitative variants result in opposing effects on the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2.
evidence: Inferred from the negative correlation observed in RILs.

claim: A reciprocal relationship was observed generally across the genome spanning five of the chromosomes.
source: While a reciprocal relationship was observed generally across the genome spanning five of the chromosomes, we observed the opposite correlation on chromosome IV (Pearson's R = 0.83, p-value=1.695×10−5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The opposite correlation was observed on chromosome IV (Pearson's R = 0.83, p-value=1.695×10−5).
source: While a reciprocal relationship was observed generally across the genome spanning five of the chromosomes, we observed the opposite correlation on chromosome IV (Pearson's R = 0.83, p-value=1.695×10−5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Pearson's R = 0.83, p-value=1.695×10−5).

claim: The N2 region on chromosome IV increased the fraction of gut in an MY16 background.
source: We found that the region affects the skn-1(RNAi) phenotype as expected: the N2 region increased the fraction of gut in an MY16 background, and the MY16 regions decreased this fraction in an N2 background.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NIL analysis.

claim: The MY16 regions on chromosome IV decreased the fraction of gut in an N2 background.
source: We found that the region affects the skn-1(RNAi) phenotype as expected: the N2 region increased the fraction of gut in an MY16 background, and the MY16 regions decreased this fraction in an N2 background.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NIL analysis.

claim: Introgressing the N2 region in MY16 dramatically changed the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype.
source: However, for mom-2(RNAi), while introgressing the N2 region in MY16 dramatically changed the phenotype (Figure 7C), we found that the MY16 region was not sufficient to alter the phenotype in an N2 background.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The MY16 region on chromosome IV was not sufficient to alter the mom-2(RNAi) phenotype in an N2 background.
source: However, for mom-2(RNAi), while introgressing the N2 region in MY16 dramatically changed the phenotype (Figure 7C), we found that the MY16 region was not sufficient to alter the phenotype in an N2 background.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NIL analysis.

claim: Replacing the N2 region with the corresponding MY16 region in all cases results in a stronger mom-2(RNAi) phenotype.
source: We created segregant NILs in which one of the genetic markers was lost (see Materials and methods) and found that replacing the N2 region with the corresponding MY16 region in all cases results in a stronger mom-2(RNAi) phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from segregant NIL analysis.

claim: For the skn-1(RNAi) phenotype, six of nine segregants showed a weaker phenotype.
source: However, for the skn-1(RNAi) phenotype six of nine segregants showed the opposite effect: that is, a weaker phenotype (Figure 7D), revealing that when contributing variants were separated by recombination, a reciprocal effect was frequently seen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: When contributing variants were separated by recombination, a reciprocal effect was frequently seen.
source: However, for the skn-1(RNAi) phenotype six of nine segregants showed the opposite effect: that is, a weaker phenotype (Figure 7D), revealing that when contributing variants were separated by recombination, a reciprocal effect was frequently seen.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that segregant NILs showed opposite effects for skn-1(RNAi) and mom-2(RNAi).

claim: Complex genetic interactions between variants on chromosome IV might mask the potential reciprocal effects that were observed on the other chromosomes.
source: These observations suggest that complex genetic interactions between variants on chromosome IV might mask the potential reciprocal effects that were observed on the other chromosomes.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the NIL analysis results.

claim: Loss of RICT-1 results in opposite effects on skn-1(-) and mom-2(-) mutants.
source: We found that loss of RICT-1, the C. elegans orthologue of the human RICTOR (Rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR; Tatebe and Shiozaki, 2017), a component of the TORC2 complex, which has been shown to antagonize SKN-1 function (Ruf et al., 2013), results in opposite effects on skn-1(-) and mom-2(-) mutants (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8A and citations (Tatebe and Shiozaki, 2017; Ruf et al., 2013).

claim: rict-1(RNAi) suppresses the absence of gut in skn-1(zu67) embryos.
source: Specifically, while rict-1(RNAi) suppresses the absence of gut in skn-1(zu67) embryos (skn-1(zu67): 34.3% ± s.d 4.1% with gut vs. skn-1(zu67); rict-1(RNAi): 48.3% ± s.d 4.9%; p=<0.001), we found that it enhances this phenotype in mom-2(or42) mutants (mom-2(or42): 23.8% ± s.d 2.0%; vs. mom-2(or42); rict-1(RNAi): 11.2% ± s.d 3.2%; p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (p=<0.001).

claim: rict-1(RNAi) enhances the gutless phenotype in mom-2(or42) mutants.
source: Specifically, while rict-1(RNAi) suppresses the absence of gut in skn-1(zu67) embryos (skn-1(zu67): 34.3% ± s.d 4.1% with gut vs. skn-1(zu67); rict-1(RNAi): 48.3% ± s.d 4.9%; p=<0.001), we found that it enhances this phenotype in mom-2(or42) mutants (mom-2(or42): 23.8% ± s.d 2.0%; vs. mom-2(or42); rict-1(RNAi): 11.2% ± s.d 3.2%; p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (p<0.001).

claim: RNAi depletion of PLP-1 reciprocally affects the outcome of removing SKN-1 and MOM-2.
source: Similarly, RNAi depletion of PLP-1, the C. elegans homologue of the Pur alpha transcription factor that has been shown to bind to and regulate the end-1 promoter (Witze et al., 2009), reciprocally affects the outcome of removing these two inputs in the same direction: loss of PLP-1 function suppresses the skn-1(-) phenotype (to 48.0% ± s.d 6.6%), and strongly enhances the mom-2 phenotype (to 6.9% ± s.d 1.6%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation (Witze et al., 2009).

claim: Loss of PLP-1 function suppresses the skn-1(-) phenotype.
source: Similarly, RNAi depletion of PLP-1, the C. elegans homologue of the Pur alpha transcription factor that has been shown to bind to and regulate the end-1 promoter (Witze et al., 2009), reciprocally affects the outcome of removing these two inputs in the same direction: loss of PLP-1 function suppresses the skn-1(-) phenotype (to 48.0% ± s.d 6.6%), and strongly enhances the mom-2 phenotype (to 6.9% ± s.d 1.6%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of PLP-1 function strongly enhances the mom-2(-) phenotype.
source: Similarly, RNAi depletion of PLP-1, the C. elegans homologue of the Pur alpha transcription factor that has been shown to bind to and regulate the end-1 promoter (Witze et al., 2009), reciprocally affects the outcome of removing these two inputs in the same direction: loss of PLP-1 function suppresses the skn-1(-) phenotype (to 48.0% ± s.d 6.6%), and strongly enhances the mom-2 phenotype (to 6.9% ± s.d 1.6%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: RICT-1, PLP-1, and MIG-5 show opposite effects on the phenotype of removing SKN-1 and MOM-2.
source: Together, these findings reveal that, as observed with many of the N2/MY16 RILs variants across most of the genome, RICT-1, PLP-1, and MIG-5 show opposite effects on the phenotype of removing SKN-1 and MOM-2, suggesting a trend toward genetic influences that reciprocally influence the outcome in the absence of these two inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing reciprocal effects.

claim: Loss of MIG-5 leads to enhancement of the skn-1(-) phenotype.
source: Loss of MIG-5 as a result of chromosomal mutation or RNAi leads to enhancement of the skn-1(-) phenotype (mig-5(rh94); skn-1(RNAi): 6.6% ± s.d 2.3%; skn-1(zu67); mig-5(RNAi): 9.4% ± s.d 1.4%) and suppression of the mom-2(-) phenotype (88.6% ± s.d 4.0%) (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8C.

claim: Loss of MIG-5 leads to suppression of the mom-2(-) phenotype.
source: Loss of MIG-5 as a result of chromosomal mutation or RNAi leads to enhancement of the skn-1(-) phenotype (mig-5(rh94); skn-1(RNAi): 6.6% ± s.d 2.3%; skn-1(zu67); mig-5(RNAi): 9.4% ± s.d 1.4%) and suppression of the mom-2(-) phenotype (88.6% ± s.d 4.0%) (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8C.

claim: The quantitative requirement for two distinct regulatory inputs that initiate expression of the endoderm GRN (SKN-1 and MOM-2) are highly reproducible in individual C. elegans isolates.
source: In this study, we report five major findings: 1) while the quantitative requirement for two distinct regulatory inputs that initiate expression of the endoderm GRN (SKN-1 and MOM-2) are highly reproducible in individual C. elegans isolates, there is wide cryptic variation between isolates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing low variability within strains and high variability between strains.

claim: There is wide cryptic variation in the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 between C. elegans isolates.
source: In this study, we report five major findings: 1) while the quantitative requirement for two distinct regulatory inputs that initiate expression of the endoderm GRN (SKN-1 and MOM-2) are highly reproducible in individual C. elegans isolates, there is wide cryptic variation between isolates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing variation across isolates.

claim: Cryptic variation in the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 shows substantial differences even between closely related strains.
source: 2) Cryptic variation in the requirement for these regulatory factors shows substantial differences even between closely related strains, suggesting that these traits are subject to rapid evolutionary change in this species.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 is subject to rapid evolutionary change in C. elegans.
source: 2) Cryptic variation in the requirement for these regulatory factors shows substantial differences even between closely related strains, suggesting that these traits are subject to rapid evolutionary change in this species.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between phylogenetic relatedness and phenotype.

claim: Multiple loci underlie the variation in the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 in endoderm specification.
source: 3) Quantitative genetic analyses of natural and recombinant populations revealed multiple loci underlying the variation in the requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 in endoderm specification.
evidence: Supported by GWAS and QTL mapping analyses.

claim: The requirements for SKN-1 and MOM-2 in endoderm specification is frequently reciprocal in their relation to other genetic factors.
source: 4) The requirements for SKN-1 and MOM-2 in endoderm specification is frequently reciprocal in their relation to other genetic factors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RILs and candidate gene analysis.

claim: rict-1, plp-1, and mig-5 reciprocally influence the outcome of skn-1(-) and mom-2(-).
source: 5) rict-1, plp-1, and mig-5 reciprocally influence the outcome of skn-1(-) and mom-2(-), substantiating the reciprocal influences on the two GRN inputs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: While the core genetic toolkit for the development of the endoderm appears to have been preserved for well over half a billion years, the molecular regulatory inputs that initiate its expression in C. elegans vary extremely rapidly over short evolutionary time scales within the species.
source: These findings reveal prevalent plasticity and complexity underlying SKN-1 and MOM-2/Wnt regulatory inputs in mobilizing a conserved system for endoderm specification. Thus, while the core genetic toolkit for the development of the endoderm, the most ancient of the three germ layers, appears to have been preserved for well over half a billion years, the molecular regulatory inputs that initiate its expression in C. elegans vary extremely rapidly over short evolutionary time scales within the species.
evidence: Inferred from the contrast between conserved downstream components and variable upstream inputs.

claim: Multigenic factors are responsible for the difference in requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 between isotypes.
source: Quantitative analyses of the wild isolates and RILs revealed that multigenic factors are responsible for the difference in requirement for SKN-1 and MOM-2 between isotypes.
evidence: Inferred from GWAS and QTL mapping results showing multiple loci.

claim: Some QTLs may influence requirement for both SKN-1 and MOM-2 inputs into the endoderm specification pathway.
source: This finding raises the possibility that some QTLs may influence requirement for both inputs into the endoderm specification pathway: as SKN-1 and Wnt converge to regulate expression of the end-1/3 genes, it is conceivable that common genetic variants might modulate the relative strength or outcome of both maternal inputs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on GWAS and QTL mapping results.

claim: Epistasis can strongly influence the behavior of certain variants upon genetic perturbation.
source: Many studies (Mackay, 2014; Volis et al., 2011; Félix, 2007; Barkoulas et al., 2013), including ours here, showed that epistasis can strongly influence the behavior of certain variants upon genetic perturbation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mackay, 2014; Volis et al., 2011; Félix, 2007; Barkoulas et al., 2013) and experimental data.

claim: Selection on pleiotropically acting loci facilitates rapid developmental system drift.
source: In addition, selection on pleiotropically acting loci facilitates rapid developmental system drift.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about evolutionary processes.

claim: Epistasis and selection on pleiotropic loci play important roles in the evolution of natural populations.
source: Together, epistasis and selection on pleiotropic loci play important roles in the evolution of natural populations (Duveau and Félix, 2012; Johnson and Porter, 2007; Phillips, 2008; Wagner and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Duveau and Félix, 2012; Johnson and Porter, 2007; Phillips, 2008; Wagner and Zhang, 2011).

claim: The SKN-1 and MOM-2/Wnt inputs might compensate for each other.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that the SKN-1 and MOM-2/Wnt inputs might compensate for each other and that genetic variants that enhance the requirement for one of the inputs may often relax the requirement for the other.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the reciprocal relationship observed in RILs and candidate gene analysis.

claim: Genetic variants that enhance the requirement for one of the inputs may often relax the requirement for the other.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that the SKN-1 and MOM-2/Wnt inputs might compensate for each other and that genetic variants that enhance the requirement for one of the inputs may often relax the requirement for the other.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the reciprocal relationship observed in RILs and candidate gene analysis.

claim: Such reciprocality could reflect cross-regulatory interactions between these two maternal inputs or could be the result of evolutionary constraints imposed by selection on these genes, which act pleiotropically in a variety of processes.
source: Such reciprocality could reflect cross-regulatory interactions between these two maternal inputs or could be the result of evolutionary constraints imposed by selection on these genes, which act pleiotropically in a variety of processes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms underlying the observed reciprocality.

claim: RICT-1 function extends lifespan in C. elegans through the action of SKN-1.
source: RICT-1 function extends lifespan in C. elegans through the action of SKN-1 (Ruf et al., 2013), and loss of RICT-1 rescues the misspecification of the MS and E blastomeres and lethality of skn-1(-) embryos (Ruf et al., 2013), consistent with our finding.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ruf et al., 2013).

claim: Loss of RICT-1 rescues the misspecification of the MS and E blastomeres and lethality of skn-1(-) embryos.
source: RICT-1 function extends lifespan in C. elegans through the action of SKN-1 (Ruf et al., 2013), and loss of RICT-1 rescues the misspecification of the MS and E blastomeres and lethality of skn-1(-) embryos (Ruf et al., 2013), consistent with our finding.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ruf et al., 2013).

claim: PLP-1 binds to the end-1 promoter and acts in parallel to the Wnt pathway and downstream of the MAPK signal.
source: We previously reported that PLP-1, a homologue of the vertebrate transcription factor pur alpha, binds to the end-1 promoter and acts in parallel to the Wnt pathway and downstream of the MAPK signal (Witze et al., 2009), thereby promoting gut formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Witze et al., 2009).

claim: PLP-1 binds at a cis regulatory site in end-1 near a putative POP-1 binding site.
source: Given that PLP-1 binds at a cis regulatory site in end-1 near a putative POP-1 binding site (Witze et al., 2009), and that SKN-1 also binds to the end-1 regulatory region (Zhu et al., 1997), it is conceivable that this reciprocality might reflect integration of information at the level of transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Witze et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 1997).

claim: SKN-1 binds to the end-1 regulatory region.
source: Given that PLP-1 binds at a cis regulatory site in end-1 near a putative POP-1 binding site (Witze et al., 2009), and that SKN-1 also binds to the end-1 regulatory region (Zhu et al., 1997), it is conceivable that this reciprocality might reflect integration of information at the level of transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Zhu et al., 1997).

claim: The reciprocality between SKN-1 and MOM-2 might reflect integration of information at the level of transcription factor binding sites.
source: Given that PLP-1 binds at a cis regulatory site in end-1 near a putative POP-1 binding site (Witze et al., 2009), and that SKN-1 also binds to the end-1 regulatory region (Zhu et al., 1997), it is conceivable that this reciprocality might reflect integration of information at the level of transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known binding sites.

claim: The architecture of the GRN is shaped by changes in cis-regulatory sequences.
source: As the architecture of the GRN is shaped by changes in cis-regulatory sequences (Peter and Davidson, 2011; Davidson and Levine, 2008), analyzing alterations in SKN-1 and Wnt/POP-1 targets among C. elegans wild isolates may provide insights into how genetic changes are accommodated without compromising the developmental output at microevolutionary time scale.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Peter and Davidson, 2011; Davidson and Levine, 2008).

claim: MIG-5 functions in the Wnt pathway in parallel to Src signaling to regulate asymmetric cell division and endoderm induction.
source: MIG-5, a dishevelled orthologue, functions in the Wnt pathway in parallel to Src signaling to regulate asymmetric cell division and endoderm induction (Bei et al., 2002; Walston et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bei et al., 2002; Walston et al., 2004).

claim: Dishevelled can play both positive and negative roles during axon guidance.
source: Recent studies showed that Dishevelled can play both positive and negative roles during axon guidance (Shafer et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Shafer et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2015).

claim: Dishevelled, upon Wnt-activation, promotes hyperphosphorylation and inactivation of Frizzled receptor to fine-tune Wnt activity.
source: Dishevelled, upon Wnt-activation, promotes hyperphosphorylation and inactivation of Frizzled receptor to fine-tune Wnt activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Dishevelled function.

claim: MIG-5 may perform similar function in EMS by downregulating activating signals (Src or MAPK), in the absence of MOM-2.
source: It is tempting to speculate that MIG-5 may perform similar function in EMS by downregulating activating signals (Src or MAPK), in the absence of MOM-2.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known Dishevelled function.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms might evolve to fine-tune the level of gut-activating regulatory inputs.
source: We hypothesize that compensatory mechanisms might evolve to fine-tune the level of gut-activating regulatory inputs.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the observed reciprocal relationships.

claim: Successful developmental events depend on tight spatial and temporal regulation of gene expression.
source: Successful developmental events depend on tight spatial and temporal regulation of gene expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about developmental biology.

claim: Anterior-posterior patterning in the Drosophila embryo is determined by the local concentrations of the Bicoid, Hunchback, and Caudal transcription factors.
source: For example, anterior-posterior patterning in the Drosophila embryo is determined by the local concentrations of the Bicoid, Hunchback, and Caudal transcription factors (Rivera-Pomar and Jäckle, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rivera-Pomar and Jäckle, 1996).

claim: SKN-1 and Wnt signaling is modulated so that the downstream genes, end-1/3, are expressed at optimal levels that ensure normal gut development.
source: We postulate that SKN-1 and Wnt signaling is modulated so that the downstream genes, end-1/3, which control specification and later differentiation of endoderm progenitors, are expressed at optimal levels that ensure normal gut development.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the observed reciprocal relationships.

claim: Suboptimal END activity leads to poorly differentiated gut and both hypo- and hyperplasia in the gut lineage.
source: Suboptimal END activity leads to poorly differentiated gut and both hypo- and hyperplasia in the gut lineage (Maduro et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2017; Maduro, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Maduro et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2017; Maduro, 2015).

claim: Hyper- or hypo-activation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in cancer development, bone diseases, and metabolic diseases.
source: Hyper- or hypo-activation of Wnt signaling has been implicated in cancer development (Zhan et al., 2017), bone diseases (Jenkins et al., 2009; Baron and Gori, 2018), and metabolic diseases (Chen and Wang, 2018; Schinner, 2009), demonstrating the importance of regulating the timing and dynamics of such developmental signals within a quantitatively restricted window.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Zhan et al., 2017; Jenkins et al., 2009; Baron and Gori, 2018; Chen and Wang, 2018; Schinner, 2009).

claim: This study revealed substantial cryptic genetic modifications that alter the relative importance of two partially redundant inputs into the C. elegans endoderm GRN, leading to rapid change in the developmental network architecture.
source: This study revealed substantial cryptic genetic modifications that alter the relative importance of two partially redundant inputs into the C. elegans endoderm GRN, leading to rapid change in the developmental network architecture (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and Figure 9.

claim: Duplicated GATA factors (the MEDs, ENDs, and ELTs) and partially redundant activating inputs (SKN-1, Wnt, Src, and MAPK) in endoderm GRN provide an opportunity for genetic variation to accumulate and 'experimentation' of new regulatory relationships without diminishing fitness.
source: In addition, duplicated GATA factors (the MEDs, ENDs, and ELTs) and partially redundant activating inputs (SKN-1, Wnt, Src, and MAPK) in endoderm GRN, provide an opportunity for genetic variation to accumulate and 'experimentation' of new regulatory relationships without diminishing fitness (Félix and Wagner, 2008; Schinner, 2009; Frankel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Félix and Wagner, 2008; Schinner, 2009; Frankel et al., 2010).

claim: Redundancy in the regulatory inputs may act to 'rescue' an initial mutation and allow for secondary mutations that might eventually lead to rewiring of the network.
source: Redundancy in the regulatory inputs may act to 'rescue' an initial mutation and allow for secondary mutations that might eventually lead to rewiring of the network.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the role of redundancy in evolution.

claim: Loss of either MyoD or Myf5 produces minimal defects in myogenesis as a result of compensatory relationship between the myogenic factors.
source: For example, loss of either MyoD or Myf5, two key regulators of muscle differentiation in metazoans, produces minimal defects in myogenesis as a result of compensatory relationship between the myogenic factors (Mohun, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mohun, 1992).

claim: Gene duplication events have resulted in an expansion of Hox genes in vertebrates to a total of >200, resulting in prevalent redundancy.
source: In vertebrates, gene duplication events have resulted in an expansion of Hox genes to a total of >200, resulting in prevalent redundancy (Imai et al., 2001; Manley and Capecchi, 1997; Nam and Nei, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Imai et al., 2001; Manley and Capecchi, 1997; Nam and Nei, 2005).

claim: The proliferation of redundant genes provides opportunities for evolutionary experimentation, subsequent specialization of new functions, and developmental system drift.
source: This proliferation of redundant genes provides opportunities for evolutionary experimentation, subsequent specialization of new functions, and developmental system drift (Nam and Nei, 2005; True and Haag, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Nam and Nei, 2005; True and Haag, 2001).

claim: In C. elegans, loss of GAP-1 or SLI-1 alone does not produce obvious defects, while double mutations lead to a multivulva phenotype.
source: In C. elegans, loss of GAP-1 (a Ras inhibitor) or SLI-1 (a negative regulator of EGFR signaling) alone does not produce obvious defects, while double mutations lead to a multivulva phenotype (Yoon et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Yoon et al., 2000).

claim: The relative importance of Ras, Notch, and Wnt signals in vulva induction differ in various genetic backgrounds and physiological conditions.
source: Notably, the relative importance of Ras, Notch, and Wnt signals in vulva induction differ in various genetic backgrounds (Milloz et al., 2008; Gleason et al., 2002) and physiological conditions (Braendle and Félix, 2008; Grimbert et al., 2018), resulting in flexibility in the system.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Milloz et al., 2008; Gleason et al., 2002; Braendle and Félix, 2008; Grimbert et al., 2018).

claim: Vulval development in C. elegans, when grown under standard laboratory conditions, predominantly favors utilization of the EGF/Ras signaling pathway.
source: While vulval development in C. elegans, when grown under standard laboratory conditions, predominantly favors utilization of the EGF/Ras signaling pathway (Braendle and Félix, 2008), Wnt is the predominant signaling pathway in the related Pristionchus pacificus, which is ~250 MY divergent (Zheng et al., 2005; Tian et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Braendle and Félix, 2008; Zheng et al., 2005; Tian et al., 2008).

claim: Wnt is the predominant signaling pathway in vulval development in Pristionchus pacificus.
source: While vulval development in C. elegans, when grown under standard laboratory conditions, predominantly favors utilization of the EGF/Ras signaling pathway (Braendle and Félix, 2008), Wnt is the predominant signaling pathway in the related Pristionchus pacificus, which is ~250 MY divergent (Zheng et al., 2005; Tian et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Zheng et al., 2005; Tian et al., 2008).

claim: Cel-lin-17 functions positively to transduce the Wnt signal.
source: In addition, while Cel-lin-17 functions positively to transduce the Wnt signal, Ppa-lin-17/Fz antagonizes Wnt signaling and instead the Wnt signal is transmitted by Ppa-lin-18/Ryk, which has acquired a novel SH3 domain not present in the C. elegans ortholog (Wang and Sommer, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wang and Sommer, 2011).

claim: Ppa-lin-17/Fz antagonizes Wnt signaling.
